Hackers have broken into Denmark’s national registry and accessed the personal information of 11,000 people, the government said on Thursday, two months after another huge data hack. Danish authorities said they had updated and modernised their security systems since the previous attack in early October, when the data of 8.8 million people was illegally accessed. Despite that, “the administration of the Civil Registration System (CPR) has discovered a new security breach,” the digital affairs ministry said. “Unauthorised third parties have accessed the CPR data of 11,000 people.” It added: “The incident was stopped thanks to a new technical monitoring system for consultations, introduced after the first incident.” Neither the perpetrators of the latest breach nor those behind the October hack have been identified yet. The supposed hacker said they had found an entry point into the register within a few hours by using the login credentials of a former employee of a small Danish company. They said the employee’s password was 123456. “The hacker says there were no security measures, such as two-factor verification, and that he was therefore able to start carrying out searches in the CPR register,” Politiken wrote at the time. These consisted of checking whether a specific identification number existed. If it did, the register would provide the name, address, date of birth, gender, date of last move and marital status of the person concerned. The suspected hacker recorded all the data but told the newspaper they had “no idea how it could be used” and did not intend to sell or disclose it. In September, the Civil Security Agency raised the threat level for cyberattacks against Denmark to “high”. There has been a surge in cyberattacks, notably targeting supermarket refrigeration systems. There has also been a series of false bomb threats against schools and planes across Europe, which could potentially be part of a hybrid warfare campaign. That theory has not been confirmed, however, due to a lack of evidence. AFP Kindly share this story:
